IRC Section 1291 PFIC excess distribution rules explained

# Section 1291 PFIC excess distribution rules explained for US expats 

Written by Mel Whitney, EA 

 Last updated May 15, 2026 

Section 1291 is the default PFIC tax regime for a US person who owns a passive foreign investment company and has not made a timely QEF or mark-to-market election. For the 2025 tax year filed in 2026, it can turn certain PFIC gains and distributions into a special tax-and-interest calculation on Form 8621, instead of normal long-term capital gain treatment.

A Section 1291 PFIC is usually taxed under the default excess distribution rules unless a valid QEF or mark-to-market election applies. A gain on sale is generally treated as an excess distribution, allocated across the holding period, taxed using prior-year highest rates, and charged interest on deferred tax.

US expats often encounter PFIC rules through non-US mutual funds, ETFs, pooled investment funds, certain foreign investment companies, and some insurance or investment wrappers. The legal test is not the product name – it is whether the foreign corporation meets the 75% passive-income test or the 50% passive-asset test under IRC §1297.

We explain the broader PFIC problem in its guide to PFIC taxes for US expats, and the filing mechanics are covered in our guide to Form 8621 for PFIC reporting.

Why Americans Abroad Should Avoid Foreign Mutual Funds

# Americans Abroad: Why You Should Avoid Foreign Funds and PFICs 

 

 By Roger Healy, MBA, CFP®, EA, TEP 

 LAST UPDATED June 23, 2022 

 

### Key Takeaways

- Foreign mutual funds, ETFs and many pooled foreign investments are usually PFICs for U.S. tax purposes.
- PFIC taxation typically converts what would be long‑term capital gains into ordinary income and adds an interest charge on “excess distributions.”
- Each PFIC generally requires a separate Form 8621 filing every year, which can add dozens of hours of compliance work and hefty tax prep fees.
- FATCA reporting by foreign financial institutions has given the IRS clear visibility into U.S. taxpayers’ foreign funds, so PFIC exposure is now very hard to hide or ignore.
- Most American expats are better off holding globally diversified investments through U.S. accounts and PFIC‑aware structures as part of a coordinated financial planning strategy.

If you’re an American living outside the United States, owning foreign mutual funds can quietly create one of the most expensive tax problems in your portfolio. These funds are usually treated as passive foreign investment companies (PFICs) under U.S. tax law, which means harsh tax treatment, ongoing interest charges and burdensome annual reporting on your U.S. tax return.

# What Is a PFIC? A Complete Guide for American Expats

If you are a U.S. person living abroad and own a foreign mutual fund, ETF, unit trust, or investment wrapper, ask whether the vehicle is a PFIC before you sell, transfer, or make an election. The classification depends on the legal entity, domicile, income and asset tests, and the relevant tax year. The rules can produce a less favorable result than ordinary capital-gain treatment, but “foreign fund” is not a complete calculation.

## The Definition

PFIC stands for Passive Foreign Investment Company. It is defined in IRC Section 1297 as any foreign corporation meeting one of two tests:

1. The Income Test: 75% or more of gross income is passive (dividends, interest, rents, royalties, capital gains).
2. The Asset Test: 50% or more of assets produce passive income or are held for the production of passive income.

For the American living abroad, the desire to integrate into the local economy is natural. You open a local bank account, perhaps buy a home, and eventually, you look to invest. You walk into a local bank in London, Paris, or Sydney, and the advisor recommends a diversified, low-cost local mutual fund or an Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF). To your local neighbors, this is a smart, standard financial move. To the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), you have just stepped into one of the most punitive tax traps in the entire U.S. Tax Code.

This trap is known as the Passive Foreign Investment Company (PFIC).

The PFIC rules for US expats were designed in the mid-1980s to prevent Americans from stashing cash in offshore shell companies to defer taxes. However, the definition was written so broadly that it captured nearly every pooled investment vehicle located outside the United States. Today, these rules represent a massive compliance burden and a significant tax threat to the global American community.

As we navigate the tax landscape, understanding how to identify, report, and manage these investments is critical for your financial survival.
